content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has established guidelines and standards for the management of biological pest control and pesticides, emphasizing the importance of minimizing hazardous substances and ensuring proper waste management. These measures are critical for safeguarding public health and the environment. The control of vector-borne diseases such as malaria, dengue, leishmaniasis, and Chagas disease remains a significant global health challenge. Malaria control efforts have intensified over the past decade, heavily relying on chemical pesticides to manage vector populations and reduce disease transmission. However, it is essential to use these pesticides responsibly to prevent adverse effects on human and animal health and the environment. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management provides voluntary standards for public and private entities involved in pesticide distribution and use. It serves as a globally accepted framework for pesticide management. Despite this, many countries, particularly those with decentralized health systems, face significant challenges in managing vector control pesticides and other public health pesticides. Even countries with long-standing vector control programs often lack the capacity to regulate pesticide availability and use effectively. Proper pesticide management throughout their life cycle—from product development to waste disposal—requires comprehensive legislation, regulatory control, operational guidelines, training, public awareness, and evaluation. The WHO project Reducing Health Risks through Sound Management of Pesticides aimed to mitigate health risks associated with pesticides by establishing national regulatory frameworks, optimizing registration procedures, strengthening post-registration monitoring and control, and reducing the trade of substandard pesticide products. The project, implemented over six years (2007–2013), was administered by the WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) in collaboration with WHO regional and country offices and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Key achievements include creating an evidence base on global pesticide registration and management practices, enhancing awareness and political support for the judicious use of public health pesticides, developing authoritative guidelines and standards, and providing technical support and training to priority countries. Global surveys conducted during the project revealed significant shortcomings in pesticide management practices, particularly in policy, capacity, quality control, and safety. These findings highlight the need for improved standards and practices to manage public health pesticides effectively and safely. The African region, in particular, lags behind the global average in many parameters. The surveys also showed that the global use of vector control insecticides is increasingly dominated by pyrethroids, raising concerns about the development of resistance to these chemicals. This is particularly critical as pyrethroids are also used in manufacturing long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), a key malaria control tool. Preserving the effectiveness of these tools through insecticide resistance management is vital. Furthermore, the global use of DDT for vector control has not declined since the Stockholm Convention came into effect in 2004. While data on vector control insecticides are available, comprehensive global data on household pesticide use are lacking and require further study. The project emphasized the importance of evidence-based strategies for improving pesticide management. Workshops and consultations held in various regions provided valuable insights and recommendations for capacity strengthening in participating countries. These efforts have been documented and published by WHO, offering a wealth of information applicable to many developing countries. In conclusion, the sound management of public health pesticides requires robust national policies, adequate budgets, and international collaboration. WHO continues to advocate for improved pesticide management practices to reduce health risks and enhance the effectiveness of vector control programs globally.
